column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: A student adds Biuret solution to a pure sample of the enzyme amylase, and the liquid turns purple. What does this result tell you about enzymes?
column14: Enzymes are proteins
column15: Enzymes are simple sugars
column16: Enzymes are fats
column17: Enzymes are made of DNA
column28: Biuret turns purple when protein is present, so the purple color shows amylase is a protein. Enzymes are proteins folded into a special 3-D shape. A common mistake is picking sugar because amylase works on starch, but what an enzyme acts on is not what it is made of.
column29: Think back to the food tests. Which macromolecule makes Biuret turn purple?

column9: Which kinds of living things use enzymes?
column14: Only humans, because people are the only ones that digest food
column15: Only animals, since plants make their own food and don't need them
column16: Only plants
column17: All living things, including plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria
column28: Every living cell runs chemical reactions, so every living thing uses enzymes. Potatoes, liver, yeast, and bacteria all have catalase, for example. A common mistake is thinking enzymes are only part of human digestion.
column29: In the potato lab, the enzyme came from a plant. What does that tell you?

column9: Sucrase is an enzyme in your small intestine. Based on its name, which molecule does sucrase most likely break down?
column14: Salt
column15: Sucrose (table sugar)
column16: Protein in meat
column17: DNA
column28: Enzymes are often named for their substrate plus -ase: sucr- + -ase acts on sucrose, table sugar. A common mistake is ignoring the first part of the name, which is the real clue.
column29: Cover up the -ase. What word is left?

column9: Lactase breaks down lactose, the sugar in milk. A student mixes lactase with sucrose (table sugar) instead. What will most likely happen?
column14: The sucrose will break down even faster than lactose would, since it is also a sugar
column15: Very little, because sucrose does not fit lactase's active site
column16: The lactase will turn into sucrase
column17: The lactase will be used up right away
column28: Enzymes are specific: lactase's active site is shaped to fit lactose, and sucrose has a different shape, so it does not fit. Students sometimes think any sugar will work because both are sugars, but the shape has to match.
column29: Think lock and key. Does a different key open the same lock?

column9: To make cheese, cooks add rennet, which contains the enzyme chymosin. Chymosin makes the proteins in milk clump into curds. What is chymosin's substrate?
column14: Milk protein
column15: Milk sugar
column16: Milk fat
column17: Water
column28: The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on, and chymosin acts on milk protein. A common mistake is choosing milk sugar because milk is famous for lactose, but lactose is lactase's substrate.
column29: The substrate is what the enzyme changes. Read what chymosin does to the milk.

column9: A ball has to be pushed up over a small hill before it can roll down the other side. If the hill is the activation energy of a reaction, what does an enzyme do?
column14: Makes the hill taller
column15: Removes the ball from the hill
column16: Makes the hill lower, so a smaller push gets the ball over
column17: Makes the valley on the other side deeper, so the ball rolls farther
column28: Enzymes lower the activation energy, the 'hill' a reaction must get over before it can start. A smaller hill means the reaction happens much faster. A common mistake is thinking enzymes add energy or change the end of the reaction, but they only lower the starting hill.
column29: Would a catalyst make it easier or harder to get over the hill?

column9: A scientist keeps a human enzyme in a water bath set to the temperature where it works fastest. Which temperature should she choose?
column28: Human enzymes work best near normal body temperature, about 37 °C. Much colder and they slow down; much hotter and they can denature. A common mistake is picking 100 °C because heat speeds reactions, but too much heat ruins an enzyme's shape.
column29: What is normal human body temperature in Celsius?

column9: Which of these would most likely stop an enzyme from working permanently?
column14: Putting it in the refrigerator overnight
column15: Boiling it for several minutes
column16: Adding more of its substrate
column17: Cutting the food it is in into smaller pieces
column28: Boiling unfolds (denatures) the enzyme, so its active site loses its shape, and that is usually permanent. Cold only slows an enzyme down; it works again when warmed. A common mistake is thinking cold destroys enzymes too.
column29: Which change ruins the enzyme's 3-D shape instead of just slowing it?

column9: In the potato lab, a student uses a bigger piece of raw potato with the same amount of hydrogen peroxide. What most likely happens?
column14: Foam forms faster, because there is more catalase
column15: Less foam forms, because the potato soaks up the peroxide
column16: Nothing changes, because the amount of enzyme does not matter
column17: The potato turns blue-black
column28: More potato means more catalase and more active sites working at once, so oxygen foam forms faster. A common mistake is thinking the amount of enzyme does not matter because enzymes are reused, but more enzyme still means more reactions at the same time.
column29: Where does the catalase come from? What happens when you have more of it?

column9: Lactose-free milk is made by adding the enzyme lactase to regular milk at the factory. Why can a person who is lactose intolerant drink it without getting sick?
column14: The lactase removed all the sugar from the milk, so there is nothing left to digest
column15: The lactase already broke the lactose into smaller sugars the person can absorb
column16: The lactase turned the lactose into fat
column17: The milk was boiled to burn off the lactose
column28: Lactase already did the job the person's body can't do: it split lactose into two smaller sugars that are easy to absorb. The milk still has sugar in it, which is why lactose-free milk tastes a little sweeter. A common mistake is thinking the sugar is removed.
column29: What job does lactase normally do in the small intestine?

column9: What job do digestive enzymes do?
column14: Break large food molecules into small ones you can absorb
column15: Store extra food as fat
column16: Carry oxygen through your blood to your muscles and organs
column17: Build strong bones and teeth by adding calcium to them as you grow
column28: Digestive enzymes break big molecules like starch, proteins, and fats into small pieces (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids) that can pass into your blood. A common mistake is mixing enzymes up with other proteins, like hemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
column29: Digestion means breaking food down. What do enzymes do to the food?

column9: Which of these is most likely the name of an enzyme?
column14: Maltose
column15: Maltase
column16: Glycogen
column17: Glycerol
column28: Most enzyme names end in -ase, so maltase is the enzyme (it breaks down maltose). Maltose ends in -ose, which usually means a sugar. A common mistake is mixing up -ose and -ase because the words look alike.
column29: Look at the last three letters of each word.

column9: Your cells make hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) as a waste product. Why is it important that cells have the enzyme catalase?
column14: It breaks harmful hydrogen peroxide into harmless water and oxygen
column15: It turns hydrogen peroxide into sugar for energy
column16: It stores hydrogen peroxide for later use
column17: It makes hydrogen peroxide stronger so it can destroy the whole cell
column28: Hydrogen peroxide is toxic to cells, and catalase quickly breaks it into water and oxygen gas, which are harmless. A common mistake is thinking the peroxide is used as food, but catalase's job is protection.
column29: What are the products in the potato lab? Are they harmful?

column9: Match each enzyme term to its meaning.
column14: Enzyme :: A protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction
column15: Substrate :: The molecule an enzyme acts on
column16: Product :: A new molecule released when the reaction is done
column17: Activation energy :: The energy needed to get a reaction started
column28: The enzyme is the protein catalyst, the substrate is what it works on, products are what come out, and activation energy is the 'hill' the enzyme lowers. A common mistake is swapping substrate and product: the substrate goes IN to the active site; products come OUT.
column29: Picture the reaction from start to finish: what goes in, what does the work, and what comes out?

column9: Match each digestive enzyme to the substrate it breaks down.
column14: Amylase :: Starch
column15: Lactase :: Lactose (milk sugar)
column16: Protease :: Proteins
column17: Lipase :: Fats and oils
column28: Many enzymes are named after their substrate: amyl- (starch), lact- (lactose), prote- (protein), lip- (lipid). A common mistake is matching amylase to proteins because amino acids also start with 'am'.
column29: Look at the beginning of each enzyme's name for a clue.

column9: In the lock-and-key model, match each part of the comparison to what it stands for.
column14: The lock :: The enzyme's active site
column15: The key :: The substrate
column16: A key that will not fit :: A molecule with the wrong shape
column17: A lock that has been bent out of shape :: A denatured enzyme
column28: The active site is the lock and the substrate is the key, so only the right shape fits. A bent lock is a denatured enzyme: even the right key will not fit anymore. A common mistake is calling the whole enzyme the key.
column29: Which molecule stays the same and gets reused, like a lock on a door?

column9: Select every molecule that is an enzyme. Select all that apply.
column14: Lactase
column15: Glucose
column16: Pepsin
column17: Catalase
column28: Lactase, pepsin, catalase, and amylase are enzymes. Pepsin is an enzyme even though its name does not end in -ase. Glucose is a sugar and cellulose is a plant polysaccharide. A common mistake is skipping pepsin because of its ending.
column29: Most enzymes end in -ase, but not all. Which of these speed up reactions?

column9: A potato that has been boiled makes almost no foam in hydrogen peroxide, because the heat has ___ its catalase.
column28: Heat denatures enzymes: it unfolds the protein so the active site loses its shape and the substrate no longer fits. A common mistake is saying the catalase was 'used up' or 'killed'; enzymes are molecules, and they lose their shape.
column29: What is the word for when a protein loses its 3-D shape?

column9: An enzyme can only bind a substrate that matches the ___ of its active site.
column28: The active site's shape has to match the substrate, like a key fitting a lock. That is why each enzyme is specific, and why changing the shape (denaturing) stops it. A common mistake is thinking it depends on the substrate's size or color.
column29: Think of a key and a lock. What has to match?

column9: Meat tenderizer powder contains papain, an enzyme from papaya fruit. Why does sprinkling it on a tough steak make the meat softer?
column14: Papain adds fat to the meat, which makes each bite juicier
column15: Papain freezes the meat
column16: Papain breaks down the proteins that make the meat tough
column17: Papain adds sugar to the meat
column28: Meat is mostly protein, and papain is a protein-digesting enzyme, so it breaks some of the tough proteins apart. A common mistake is picking 'adds fat'; enzymes change their substrate, they do not add new ingredients.
column29: Meat is made mostly of which macromolecule?

column9: Your stomach makes pepsin to digest the proteins in a cheeseburger. Why doesn't pepsin also digest the fat in the cheeseburger?
column14: Fat molecules don't fit pepsin's active site
column15: Pepsin gets used up on the proteins first
column16: Fat is not part of food
column17: Pepsin only works on cold food
column28: Each enzyme is specific: pepsin's active site fits proteins, not fats. A different enzyme, lipase, handles fats. A common mistake is thinking the enzyme runs out; enzymes are reused, so that is not the reason.
column29: Why does a key open only one lock?

column9: When a person's body temperature falls well below normal (hypothermia), the chemical reactions in their cells slow down. Why?
column14: The cold denatures all of their enzymes so they stop working
column15: Their enzymes work more slowly when it is colder
column16: The body runs out of enzymes
column17: The cold creates extra substrate
column28: Cold slows molecules down, so enzymes and substrates meet less often and reactions slow. That is why hypothermia is dangerous. A common mistake is saying cold denatures enzymes; too much heat does that, while cold only slows them.
column29: Do molecules move faster or slower when it's cold?

column9: The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest is called its ___ temperature.
column28: The optimum temperature is the peak of an enzyme-activity graph, where the enzyme works fastest. For most human enzymes it is about 37 °C. A common mistake is writing 'maximum', but the hottest temperature is not the best one.
column29: It's the word for the best conditions, the top of the curve.

column9: Why does your body need enzymes?
column14: They make chemical reactions fast enough at body temperature to keep you alive
column15: They make your body warmer so that reactions can happen fast enough to keep you alive
column16: They are only needed when you have a fever
column17: They slow reactions down so you don't use too much energy
column28: Without enzymes, most reactions in your cells would be far too slow at 37 °C. Enzymes speed them up without needing extra heat. A common mistake is thinking enzymes slow things down or heat the body.
column29: What does a catalyst do to the speed of a reaction?

column9: Enzymes can help build larger molecules, not just break molecules apart.
column28: True. In the active site, bonds can be broken or built. Some enzymes split molecules (like amylase on starch) and others join small molecules into bigger ones. A common mistake is thinking enzymes only do digestion.
column29: In the enzyme-substrate complex, what can happen to bonds?

column9: Select every job that enzymes do in the human body. Select all that apply.
column14: Break down food molecules during digestion
column15: Speed up the reactions that release energy from glucose in cells
column16: Carry oxygen in red blood cells
column17: Store genetic information
column18: Form the walls of plant cells
column28: Enzymes speed up reactions, like digesting food and releasing energy from glucose. Hemoglobin (not an enzyme) carries oxygen, DNA stores genetic information, and cellulose forms plant cell walls. A common mistake is choosing hemoglobin because it is also a protein.
column29: Enzymes speed up reactions. Which choices are reactions?

column9: Two test tubes each get 5 mL of hydrogen peroxide. Tube A also gets a cube of raw potato. Tube B gets nothing else. What is Tube B?
column14: The control
column15: The independent variable
column16: The enzyme
column17: The product
column28: Tube B is the control. It shows what hydrogen peroxide does with no enzyme, so you can compare. A common mistake is calling it the independent variable, which is the thing you change on purpose (adding potato).
column29: Which tube is used for comparison?

column9: Put the steps of an enzyme reaction in order.
column14: The substrate fits into the active site
column15: The products are released
column16: The enzyme and substrate move close together
column17: Bonds are broken or built while the substrate is held in the enzyme-substrate complex
column18: The unchanged enzyme is ready for a new substrate
column28: Enzyme and substrate meet → substrate fits the active site → bonds change in the enzyme-substrate complex → products are released → the enzyme is reused. A common mistake is putting 'products released' before the enzyme-substrate complex forms.
column29: The enzyme can't change the substrate until the substrate is in the active site.

column9: A student wants to test a human enzyme at its best temperature. Her water bath is at 25 °C. How many degrees Celsius warmer must she make it?
column28: Human enzymes work best near 37 °C, and 37 − 25 = 12 degrees warmer. A common mistake is using 98.6, which is body temperature in Fahrenheit, not Celsius.
column29: First recall the optimum temperature for human enzymes in °C, then subtract.

column9: Laundry detergents with enzymes break down protein stains like grass, egg, and blood. The label says to wash in warm water, not boiling water. Why?
column14: Enzymes need ice-cold water to start working on tough stains
column15: Boiling water would unfold the enzymes so they stop working
column16: Warm water makes the stains bigger
column17: Boiling water would add extra enzymes
column28: Very hot water denatures the enzymes, so they lose their shape and stop working. Warm water lets them work near their best temperature. A common mistake is thinking hotter always cleans better, which is not true for enzymes.
column29: Enzymes are proteins. What does very high heat do to proteins?

column9: Fireflies glow because the enzyme luciferase speeds up a light-making reaction. If a firefly's luciferase lost its 3-D shape, what would most likely happen?
column14: The firefly would glow brighter
column15: The firefly would glow a different color, because the enzyme now does a new job
column16: The firefly could not glow well, because the substrate would no longer fit
column17: Nothing, because shape does not matter to enzymes
column28: An enzyme's shape is its function. If luciferase loses its shape, its active site no longer fits the substrate, so the light reaction slows or stops. A common mistake is thinking a changed enzyme does a different job.
column29: Remember: change the shape, lose the job.

column9: Which test tube would make the MOST foam?
column14: Raw potato in hydrogen peroxide at room temperature
column15: Boiled potato in hydrogen peroxide at room temperature
column16: Raw potato in plain water
column17: Hydrogen peroxide with no potato
column28: You need both working catalase (raw potato) and its substrate (hydrogen peroxide) to make lots of oxygen foam. Boiled potato has denatured catalase, plain water has no substrate, and peroxide alone breaks down very slowly. A common mistake is forgetting that the enzyme needs its substrate.
column29: Which tube has both a working enzyme and its substrate?

column9: Select every product made when lactase breaks down lactose. Select all that apply.
column14: Glucose
column15: Fructose
column16: Galactose
column17: Maltose
column28: Lactose is glucose + galactose, so lactase splits it into those two sugars. Fructose comes from sucrose, maltose is a different double sugar, and amino acids come from proteins. A common mistake is choosing fructose because it is in table sugar.
column29: Milk sugar is made of glucose plus one other single sugar. Which one?

column9: Enzymes are not used up, so one enzyme molecule can work again and again. If one enzyme molecule breaks down 50 substrate molecules every second, how many substrate molecules does it break down in 10 seconds?
column28: 50 molecules per second × 10 seconds = 500 molecules. Because the enzyme is reused, it keeps going at the same rate. A common mistake is answering 50, as if the enzyme stopped after one round.
column29: Multiply the number per second by the number of seconds.

column9: Why does chewing your food well help your digestive enzymes work faster?
column14: Chewing adds heat to the food that speeds up the enzymes in your mouth
column15: Chewing makes smaller pieces, so more surface is open to enzymes
column16: Chewing turns starch into protein
column17: Chewing makes new enzymes
column28: Smaller pieces have more surface area, so more substrate molecules can reach the enzymes' active sites at once. A common mistake is thinking chewing heats food enough to matter; the real reason is surface area.
column29: Is it easier for enzymes to reach food in one big chunk or many small pieces?

column9: Which word describes the fact that each enzyme works on only one kind of substrate?
column14: Specific
column15: Denatured
column16: Acidic
column17: Saturated
column28: Enzymes are specific: each active site fits one substrate, like one key for one lock. Denatured means the enzyme lost its shape. A common mistake is choosing 'saturated', which describes fats or a solution that can't hold more.
column29: Think of the phrase 'one key, one lock'.

column9: A student drops a raw potato cube into hydrogen peroxide and the liquid fizzes and foams. What is the foam evidence of?
column14: A chemical reaction sped up by an enzyme
column15: The potato dissolving in water
column16: The liquid boiling
column17: The potato making new hydrogen peroxide
column28: The bubbles are a new substance, oxygen gas, so a chemical reaction is happening, and catalase from the potato is speeding it up. A common mistake is saying the liquid is boiling; it is not hot, it is releasing oxygen.
column29: Is a new gas being made? What made it happen so fast?

column9: What gives each enzyme its own special shape?
column14: The order of its amino acids and the way that chain folds
column15: The amount of water in the cell
column16: The color of the food it digests
column17: The substrate it will act on later, which molds the enzyme around it
column28: An enzyme is a protein: its amino acid order is set by a gene, and that chain folds into a 3-D shape with an active site. A common mistake is thinking the substrate shapes the enzyme; the enzyme already has its shape before the substrate arrives.
column29: Enzymes are proteins. What are proteins built from, and what do those chains do?

column9: Which of these is a substrate, not an enzyme?
column14: Lactase
column15: Amylase
column16: Lactose
column17: Catalase
column28: Lactose (milk sugar) is a substrate; it is what lactase acts on. The -ose ending usually means a sugar, and -ase means an enzyme. A common mistake is mixing up lactose and lactase.
column29: Look at the endings: -ose or -ase?

column9: Some fish live deep in the ocean, where the water is about 4 °C all year. What would you predict about their enzymes?
column14: They probably work best at cold temperatures
column15: They work best at 37 °C, the same temperature as human enzymes
column16: These fish do not have enzymes
column17: They work best at 100 °C
column28: Each organism's enzymes are adapted to the temperature where it lives, so cold-water fish have enzymes with a low optimum. A common mistake is thinking every enzyme works best at 37 °C; that is true for humans, not all living things.
column29: Human enzymes work best at human body temperature. Apply the same idea to the fish.

column9: Before a cell divides, the enzyme DNA polymerase helps copy the cell's DNA. If this enzyme stopped working, what would most likely happen?
column14: The cell would divide faster, since it skips the copying step
column15: Digestion would stop
column16: The cell could not copy its DNA well enough to divide
column17: Nothing, because DNA copies itself without help from any enzyme
column28: DNA polymerase speeds up the reactions that copy DNA. Without it, copying would be far too slow, and the cell could not divide properly. A common mistake is thinking enzymes only matter for digestion.
column29: What reaction does this enzyme speed up?

column9: Your body makes thousands of different kinds of enzymes. Why does it need so many?
column14: Each enzyme speeds up only one specific reaction
column15: Enzymes are used up after each reaction, so the body needs many backups
column16: Each enzyme works only once a day
column17: Having more kinds of enzymes keeps you warmer by making extra body heat
column28: Because each enzyme is specific to one substrate and reaction, the body needs a different enzyme for each job. A common mistake is thinking enzymes are used up; they are reused, so that is not why there are so many.
column29: Can one key open every lock in a building?

column9: Bread dough rises because yeast cells use enzymes to break down sugar and release carbon dioxide gas. Why does dough rise faster in a warm kitchen than in a cold one?
column14: Warm air adds sugar to the dough
column15: Cold temperatures destroy the yeast's enzymes forever, so the dough can never rise
column16: Yeast enzymes work faster when it is warmer, up to their best temperature
column17: Dough only rises in the cold
column28: Warming speeds up enzymes (up to their optimum) because molecules move faster and meet more often, so more gas forms. A common mistake is thinking cold destroys enzymes; it only slows them.
column29: How does temperature affect the speed of molecules?

column9: In three trials, raw potato in hydrogen peroxide made foam that was 22 mm, 26 mm, and 24 mm tall. What is the average foam height in mm?
column28: Add the trials and divide by the number of trials: (22 + 26 + 24) ÷ 3 = 72 ÷ 3 = 24 mm. A common mistake is dividing by 2 or forgetting to divide at all.
column29: Add all three, then divide by how many trials there were.

column9: Which of these is a chemical reaction that an enzyme speeds up in your body?
column14: Sweat evaporating from your skin to cool you down
column15: Ice melting in your drink
column16: Starch being broken into sugars during digestion
column17: Sound waves traveling into your ear
column28: Breaking starch into sugars makes new substances, so it is a chemical reaction, and amylase speeds it up. Evaporating and melting are physical changes, and sound traveling into your ear is not a chemical reaction at all. A common mistake is choosing sweat because it happens in the body.
column29: Which choice makes a new substance?

column9: Gelatin desserts (made of protein) will not set if you add fresh pineapple, but canned pineapple works fine. Fresh pineapple contains bromelain, a protein-digesting enzyme. Canned pineapple is heated during canning. Why does canned pineapple work?
column14: Canning adds extra gelatin to the fruit
column15: The heat of canning denatured the bromelain
column16: Canned pineapple has more bromelain, which helps the gelatin set
column17: Bromelain only works on cold gelatin
column28: Heating during canning denatures bromelain, so it can no longer digest the gelatin protein and the dessert sets. A common mistake is thinking canned fruit has 'no enzymes' to begin with; it had them, but heat changed their shape.
column29: What does high heat do to an enzyme's shape?

column9: Two pieces of raw potato have the same mass. One is a single cube; the other is chopped into tiny pieces. Both go into equal amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Which makes foam faster, and why?
column14: The tiny pieces, because more catalase is exposed to the hydrogen peroxide
column15: The single cube, because it holds more enzyme
column16: Both the same, because the mass is the same
column17: The single cube, because chopping denatures catalase and slows the reaction
column28: Chopping does not add catalase, but it exposes more surface, so more enzyme can reach the substrate at once. A common mistake is thinking equal mass means equal speed; how much enzyme can touch the substrate matters too.
column29: Where can the hydrogen peroxide reach the catalase: inside the potato, or on its surface?

column9: A potato cube in hydrogen peroxide foams for a while, then stops. A student pours off the liquid and adds fresh hydrogen peroxide to the same cube. It foams again. What does this show?
column14: The catalase was not used up; the substrate ran out
column15: The potato made new hydrogen peroxide while the tube sat empty
column16: The catalase multiplied while it waited, making more enzyme
column17: The first hydrogen peroxide was too cold
column28: Foaming stopped because the hydrogen peroxide (substrate) was used up, not the enzyme. Fresh substrate restarted the reaction with the same catalase. A common mistake is saying the enzyme 'ran out'.
column29: What was replaced: the enzyme or the substrate?

column9: A potato cube is soaked in vinegar (pH about 3) for 10 minutes and then dropped into hydrogen peroxide. It makes much less foam than an untreated cube. What is the best explanation?
column14: The vinegar added more substrate
column15: The vinegar is an enzyme that competes with catalase for the hydrogen peroxide
column16: The acid changed catalase's shape, so the substrate doesn't fit as well
column17: The vinegar made the potato bigger
column28: Catalase works best near neutral pH. Strong acid changes its shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate well, and less oxygen forms. A common mistake is thinking acid 'kills' the potato; the key idea is the enzyme's shape.
column29: Each enzyme has a pH it works best at. What happens to shape far from it?

column9: A human digestive enzyme is working at normal body temperature and its best pH. Select every change that would make it work SLOWER. Select all that apply.
column14: Cooling it to 10 °C
column15: Heating it to 65 °C
column16: Changing the pH far from its best pH
column17: Adding more of the same enzyme
column18: Adding more substrate when there is not much yet
column28: Cooling slows molecules down, too much heat denatures the enzyme, and a pH far from optimum changes its shape. Adding more enzyme or more substrate (when substrate is low) speeds the reaction up. A common mistake is thinking any change from normal slows an enzyme.
column29: It's already at its best temperature and pH. Which changes move it away from best?

column9: A test tube has plenty of substrate. A student doubles the amount of enzyme in the tube. What most likely happens to the reaction rate?
column14: It decreases, because the extra enzymes crowd each other out
column15: It stays the same, because enzymes are reused
column16: It increases, because more active sites are working at once
column17: It drops to zero
column28: With plenty of substrate, more enzyme means more active sites working at the same time, so the rate goes up. A common mistake is thinking reuse means the amount doesn't matter; reuse explains why a little enzyme goes far, not why more enzyme doesn't help.
column29: Is the substrate or the enzyme in short supply here?

column9: In 4 minutes, a potato cube in hydrogen peroxide made a column of foam 36 mm tall. What was the average rate, in mm of foam per minute?
column28: Rate = amount ÷ time = 36 mm ÷ 4 min = 9 mm per minute. A common mistake is multiplying (36 × 4 = 144) instead of dividing.
column29: A rate is 'how much per minute'. Divide the foam by the time.

column9: Catalase speeds up this reaction: 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. If 10 molecules of hydrogen peroxide break down, how many molecules of oxygen gas (O₂) are made?
column28: The equation shows 2 H₂O₂ make 1 O₂. So 10 H₂O₂ make 10 ÷ 2 = 5 O₂. A common mistake is answering 10, as if each H₂O₂ made its own O₂.
column29: How many H₂O₂ molecules does it take to make one O₂?

column9: Match each condition to what happens to an enzyme.
column14: Heated far above its optimum :: Unfolds and stops working, usually for good
column15: pH far from its optimum :: Active site changes shape and the substrate fits poorly
column16: At its optimum temperature and pH :: Works at its fastest rate
column17: Every active site already busy :: Adding more substrate no longer speeds it up
column28: Heat and the wrong pH both change the enzyme's shape. At the optimum it is fastest. When every active site is busy, extra substrate has to wait its turn. A common mistake is mixing up 'busy active sites' with denaturing; a busy enzyme still has its shape.
column29: Decide which conditions change the enzyme's shape and which do not.

column9: Match each substrate to the smaller molecules a digestive enzyme breaks it into.
column14: Starch :: Many small sugar units
column15: Protein :: Amino acids
column16: Fat (triglyceride) :: Glycerol and fatty acids
column17: Sucrose :: Glucose and fructose
column28: Enzymes break polymers into their building blocks: starch into sugars, proteins into amino acids, fats into glycerol and fatty acids. Sucrose splits into glucose + fructose and maltose into glucose + glucose. A common mistake is giving fats amino acids; amino acids only come from proteins.
column29: Think about the monomers of each macromolecule from LT4.

column9: A human enzyme is slowly heated from 10 °C to 70 °C. Put what happens in order.
column14: Its shape starts to change and the rate drops quickly
column15: It works slowly because the molecules move slowly
column16: It reaches its fastest rate at the optimum temperature
column17: The rate rises as molecules move faster and meet more often
column18: It is fully denatured and the rate is near zero
column28: Slow when cold → faster as it warms → peak at the optimum → shape starts to change past the optimum → fully denatured. A common mistake is thinking the rate keeps rising forever with heat.
column29: Picture the temperature graph: up the left side, the peak, then down the right side.

column9: Put these events in order for a person who drinks a glass of milk.
column14: Lactase binds lactose in its active site
column15: The person drinks the milk
column16: The two smaller sugars are absorbed into the blood
column17: Lactose reaches the small intestine
column18: The bond holding lactose together is broken
column28: Drink → lactose reaches the small intestine → lactase binds it → the bond breaks → the smaller sugars are absorbed. A common mistake is putting absorption before the bond is broken; lactose is too big to absorb whole.
column29: Food has to be broken down before it can be absorbed.

column9: Put the steps of the potato catalase lab in order.
column14: Measure the height of the foam in each tube
column15: Pour 10 mL of hydrogen peroxide into each test tube
column16: Drop a raw potato cube into the hydrogen peroxide in the experimental tube only
column17: Wait 2 minutes
column18: Compare the foam heights to draw a conclusion
column28: Set up the substrate → add the enzyme to the experimental tube → wait a set time → measure → compare. A common mistake is measuring before waiting the same time in each tube, which makes it an unfair test.
column29: You can't measure foam until the enzyme has had time to work.

column9: A student tested potato catalase at different temperatures and measured the foam: 10 °C = 12 mm, 25 °C = 24 mm, 40 °C = 38 mm, 55 °C = 15 mm, 70 °C = 2 mm. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Catalase activity always increases with temperature, since foam rose at first
column15: Temperature does not affect catalase
column16: Catalase works best at 70 °C
column17: Activity rises to a peak near 40 °C and falls at higher temperatures
column28: Foam rises from 10 °C to a peak at 40 °C, then drops sharply as the enzyme starts to denature. A common mistake is reading only the first few numbers and concluding 'hotter is always better'.
column29: Find the biggest number, then look at what happens on each side of it.

column9: Catalase from potatoes, from liver, and from yeast all break down hydrogen peroxide, even though they come from very different organisms. What do these catalase enzymes most likely have in common?
column14: They come from the same kind of cell
column15: An active site shaped to fit hydrogen peroxide
column16: They all need sunlight to work
column17: They are all exactly the same size as a potato cell
column28: Because each enzyme is specific, any enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide needs an active site that fits hydrogen peroxide. A common mistake is choosing 'same kind of cell'; plants, animals, and fungi have different cells but similar enzymes for the same job.
column29: What part of an enzyme decides which substrate it works on?

column9: Amylase breaks down starch, but it cannot break down cellulose (plant fiber), even though both are made of glucose. What is the best explanation?
column14: Cellulose has a different shape, so it doesn't fit amylase's active site
column15: Cellulose is a protein
column16: Amylase gets used up on starch first, so none is left over for the cellulose
column17: Cellulose molecules are too small
column28: Starch and cellulose have the same glucose units joined by different links, which gives them different shapes. Amylase's active site fits starch's shape only. A common mistake is thinking 'both are glucose' means one enzyme works on both, but shape is what matters.
column29: Same building blocks, different connections. What does that do to the shape?

column9: An energy diagram shows the same reaction twice: once with an enzyme and once without. How is the line for the enzyme reaction different?
column14: The hill at the start is lower
column15: The hill at the start is higher
column16: The products end up with more energy
column17: It starts with different reactants
column28: The enzyme lowers the activation energy, so the hill is shorter; the starting and ending energies stay the same. A common mistake is thinking the enzyme changes the products or their energy.
column29: What does an enzyme lower?

column9: A student wrote five claims about enzymes. Select every claim that is correct. Select all that apply.
column14: An enzyme can be reused many times
column15: Enzymes are only found in the digestive system
column16: Enzymes are used up as the reaction runs
column17: Each enzyme speeds up a specific reaction
column28: Enzymes are reused and specific. They are found in every cell, not just the gut, they are not used up, and they are molecules, not living things. A common mistake is calling a denatured enzyme 'dead', which suggests enzymes are alive.
column29: Think about what happens to an enzyme after the reaction, and where enzymes are found.

column9: Two students mix amylase with starch. Student 1 keeps her tube at 37 °C, and Student 2 keeps his at 20 °C. Both tubes eventually show no starch in an iodine test, but Student 2's tube takes much longer. What explains this?
column14: 20 °C denatured Student 2's amylase, so it worked more slowly
column15: The lower temperature slowed the amylase but did not stop it
column16: Student 2's amylase was used up
column17: Iodine does not work at 20 °C
column28: At 20 °C molecules move more slowly, so amylase works more slowly, but it still finishes the job. If it were denatured, the starch would never disappear. A common mistake is thinking any temperature below 37 °C denatures a human enzyme.
column29: Did Student 2's amylase finish the job eventually? What does that tell you?

column9: A person who is lactose intolerant eats a cheese pizza and takes a pill containing amylase instead of lactase. Will the pill prevent their symptoms?
column14: Yes, because any digestive enzyme can digest any kind of sugar
column15: Yes, because both enzyme names end in -ase, so they do the same job
column16: No, because amylase digests starch and only lactase fits lactose
column17: No, because pills can't contain enzymes
column28: Enzymes are specific: amylase's active site fits starch, not lactose, so the milk sugar would still go undigested. A common mistake is thinking all digestive enzymes are interchangeable.
column29: Which enzyme's active site matches milk sugar?

column9: While the substrate is bound in the active site, the enzyme and substrate together are called the enzyme-___ complex.
column28: The enzyme-substrate complex is the moment the substrate is held in the active site and its bonds are broken or built. A common mistake is writing 'product'; products are released after the complex.
column29: It's named for the two molecules that are stuck together.

column9: A student wants to show that lactase is specific. Which experiment would test this best?
column14: Heat one tube of lactase and leave one at room temperature, then compare how well they work
column15: Mix lactase with lactose in one tube and sucrose in another, then see which breaks down
column16: Add more and more lactase to a tube of lactose
column17: Change the pH of a lactase tube
column28: To test specificity, give the same enzyme two different substrates and see which one it works on. The other choices test temperature, amount, or pH. A common mistake is picking the heat test, which tests denaturing, not specificity.
column29: Specific means it works on only one substrate. What should you change between tubes?

column9: Fresh kiwi contains actinidin, a protein-digesting enzyme. A cook marinates chicken in kiwi puree. After 30 minutes the chicken is tender, but after 8 hours it is mushy. Why?
column14: The enzyme multiplied in the chicken
column15: The enzyme is not used up, so it kept breaking down proteins the whole time
column16: The enzyme denatured after 30 minutes, and the denatured enzyme turned the chicken to mush
column17: Kiwi sugar dissolved the meat
column28: Enzymes are reused, so actinidin keeps digesting protein for as long as it touches the meat. Too much time means too much protein broken down. A common mistake is thinking enzymes multiply; they are molecules, not living things.
column29: What happens to an enzyme after it finishes one reaction?

column9: A student mixes salivary amylase and starch at 37 °C in three tubes at pH 2, pH 7, and pH 12. After 10 minutes, iodine turns blue-black in the pH 2 and pH 12 tubes and stays yellow-brown in the pH 7 tube. What does this show?
column14: Amylase works best in strong acid
column15: pH does not affect amylase
column16: Amylase broke down the starch at pH 7 but not at the extreme pHs
column17: The iodine broke down the starch at pH 7, which is why it stayed yellow-brown
column28: Blue-black means starch is still there; yellow-brown means it was digested. Only the pH 7 tube lost its starch, so amylase worked there but not at pH 2 or 12. A common mistake is reading blue-black as 'the enzyme worked'.
column29: First decide what each iodine color means about starch.

column9: In the floating-disk lab, a paper disk soaked in catalase sinks in hydrogen peroxide and then floats up as oxygen bubbles form. A disk with raw catalase rose in 8 seconds. A disk with catalase that had been heated rose in 40 seconds. How many times longer did the heated disk take?
column28: 40 s ÷ 8 s = 5 times longer. Heating denatured some of the catalase, so oxygen formed more slowly. A common mistake is subtracting (40 − 8 = 32), which gives how many seconds longer, not how many times longer.
column29: 'How many times' means divide the larger time by the smaller time.

column9: A classmate says, "If I add a lot more enzyme, the reaction will keep going forever, even after the substrate is gone." What is wrong with this idea?
column14: Enzymes slow reactions down
column15: Once the substrate is used up, there is nothing left to react, so it stops
column16: Adding more enzyme always makes the reaction slower, so it would stop sooner
column17: The enzyme turns into new substrate
column28: An enzyme only speeds up the change of its substrate. With no substrate left, there is nothing to react, no matter how much enzyme is there. A common mistake is thinking enzymes make products out of nothing.
column29: What does the enzyme need in its active site to make products?

column9: A student is testing whether temperature affects catalase. Select every variable she should keep the SAME in every tube. Select all that apply.
column14: The amount of hydrogen peroxide
column15: The size of the potato piece
column16: The temperature of each tube
column17: The time she waits before measuring foam
column28: Temperature is the independent variable, so it is the one thing that changes. Everything else (amount of peroxide, potato size, time, kind of potato) must stay the same for a fair test. A common mistake is keeping temperature constant too, which leaves nothing being tested.
column29: Which variable is she testing? Everything else is a constant.

column9: A patient's pancreas stops releasing digestive enzymes into the small intestine. Which problem would doctors most likely expect?
column14: Food would not be fully digested, so the person couldn't absorb enough nutrients
column15: The person would digest food faster than normal, since enzymes slow digestion down
column16: The person's stomach acid would become basic
column17: Nothing would change, because the stomach does all digestion
column28: Pancreatic enzymes break down starch, proteins, and fats in the small intestine. Without them, large food molecules can't be absorbed, so the person can become malnourished. A common mistake is thinking the stomach digests everything by itself.
column29: What happens to food molecules that never get broken down?

column9: A student puts a boiled potato cube into hydrogen peroxide, and almost no foam forms. She then drops a raw potato cube into the same tube. What will most likely happen?
column14: Lots of foam forms, because the raw potato has working catalase
column15: No foam forms, because the boiled potato blocks the reaction
column16: Foam forms only if the tube is boiled again
column17: No foam forms, because the hydrogen peroxide was already used up
column28: The boiled potato's catalase was denatured, so it barely used any hydrogen peroxide. The raw potato brings working catalase to all that leftover substrate. A common mistake is thinking the peroxide was used up, but almost no reaction happened.
column29: Was much substrate used up in the first part? What does the raw potato add?

column9: Hydrogen peroxide in a bottle slowly breaks down into water and oxygen by itself over many months. With a piece of potato, it breaks down in seconds. What does this show about catalase?
column14: Catalase makes a reaction possible that could never happen at all without it
column15: Catalase speeds up a reaction that would happen anyway, just very slowly
column16: Catalase is one of the products
column17: Catalase only works in the dark
column28: Enzymes do not make impossible reactions happen; they speed up reactions that would otherwise be far too slow by lowering activation energy. A common mistake is thinking the reaction can't happen at all without the enzyme.
column29: Did the reaction happen in the bottle without any potato?

column9: One sample of an enzyme was held at 70 °C for 10 minutes, then cooled to 37 °C and tested: it had 2% of its normal activity. Another sample was held at 0 °C for 10 minutes, then warmed to 37 °C: it had 98% of its normal activity. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The heat caused lasting damage to the enzyme's shape, but the cold did not
column15: The cold damaged the enzyme more than the heat did, since 0 °C is farther from 37 °C
column16: Both temperatures permanently destroyed the enzyme
column17: Temperature has no effect on this enzyme
column28: After cooling back to 37 °C, the heated sample still barely worked, so its shape was permanently changed (denatured). The cold sample recovered almost fully, so cold only slowed it. A common mistake is assuming any extreme temperature has the same effect.
column29: Both samples were tested at 37 °C afterward. Which one recovered?

column9: Before freezing green beans, cooks often dip them in boiling water for 2 minutes. This stops enzymes that would slowly ruin the beans' color and flavor in the freezer. Why doesn't freezing alone solve the problem?
column14: Freezing speeds up the enzymes
column15: Freezing only slows the enzymes, so they keep working slowly for months
column16: Freezing denatures the enzymes, but they come back to life when they thaw
column17: Boiling adds more enzymes that protect the beans
column28: Cold slows enzymes but does not destroy their shape, so over months in the freezer they still do damage. A quick boil denatures them so they stop for good. A common mistake is thinking freezing stops all enzyme activity.
column29: Which does cold do to an enzyme: slow it down or change its shape?

column9: In a catalase lab, raw potato made 50 mL of oxygen at 37 °C. The same setup at 10 °C made 20 mL in the same time. What percent of the 37 °C amount was made at 10 °C?
column28: Percent = part ÷ whole × 100 = 20 ÷ 50 × 100 = 40%. A common mistake is dividing the other way (50 ÷ 20 = 2.5) or subtracting (50 − 20 = 30).
column29: The 37 °C amount is the whole. Divide the 10 °C amount by it and multiply by 100.

column9: A student tests catalase at 0, 20, 40, 60, and 80 °C. The 40 °C tube makes the most foam, but she used a larger piece of potato in that tube than in the others. Why can't she conclude that 40 °C is the best temperature?
column14: She needed to test more than five temperatures to find the best one
column15: She changed two variables, the temperature and the potato size
column16: Potatoes do not contain catalase
column17: 40 °C is too cold for any enzyme
column28: She changed both temperature and the amount of enzyme in the 40 °C tube, so she can't tell which one caused more foam. A fair test changes only one variable. A common mistake is thinking more trials fixes it; the real problem is the uncontrolled variable.
column29: In a fair test, how many variables should change at once?

column9: A student adds more and more substrate to a tube with a fixed amount of enzyme. The rate rises, then levels off. Once it is level, she adds more ENZYME. What will most likely happen to the rate?
column14: It will rise again, because more active sites are now available
column15: It will stay level, because the enzyme is already at its optimum
column16: It will drop, because the enzymes will compete for substrate
column17: It will drop to zero, because the extra enzyme denatures
column28: The rate leveled off because every active site was busy; the enzyme was the limit. Adding enzyme adds active sites, so the rate climbs again. A common mistake is thinking the level part of the graph means the reaction can't go any faster no matter what.
column29: When the rate was level, what was in short supply: substrate or active sites?

column9: People who are lactose intolerant often get gas and cramps after drinking milk. What causes these symptoms?
column14: Lactase makes gas as a waste product when it breaks down lactose in the stomach
column15: Bacteria in the large intestine feed on the undigested lactose and make gas
column16: Lactose turns into fat in the stomach
column17: Milk makes stomach acid become basic
column28: Without enough lactase, lactose stays whole and can't be absorbed in the small intestine. It moves to the large intestine, where bacteria break it down and release gas. A common mistake is blaming the enzyme; the problem is the missing enzyme.
column29: If lactose isn't broken down and absorbed, where does it go next?

column9: A human enzyme's reaction rate was measured: 10 °C = 8, 20 °C = 16, 30 °C = 28, 37 °C = 35, 45 °C = 20, 55 °C = 4. Select every statement this data supports. Select all that apply.
column14: The optimum temperature is about 37 °C
column15: The enzyme works faster at 20 °C than at 10 °C
column16: At 55 °C, most of the enzyme has probably lost its shape
column17: The rate at 45 °C is higher than the rate at 30 °C
column18: Warming from 10 °C to 30 °C denatured the enzyme
column28: The peak (35) is at 37 °C, the rate doubles from 10 °C to 20 °C, and the crash to 4 at 55 °C fits denaturing. At 45 °C the rate is 20, which is lower than 28 at 30 °C, and the rate rose from 10 to 30 °C, so it was not denatured there. A common mistake is assuming the rate is higher on the hot side of the peak.
column29: Check each statement against the actual numbers.

column9: A student claims, "Enzymes speed up reactions by giving them extra energy." Which evidence best shows this claim is wrong?
column14: Enzymes are made of protein, built from chains of amino acids
column15: The total energy released is the same with or without the enzyme
column16: Enzymes have an active site where the substrate fits during the reaction
column17: Enzymes are found in every cell
column28: If enzymes added energy, the reaction's energy would change. Instead, the starting and ending energies stay the same and only the activation-energy hill gets lower. The other choices are true facts but don't address energy. A common mistake is choosing a true statement that doesn't test the claim.
column29: Which choice is about energy?

column9: Tube A has a potato cube in 5 mL of hydrogen peroxide. Tube B has an identical cube in 20 mL. Tube A foams for 2 minutes and stops; Tube B foams for 8 minutes. Why did Tube A stop first?
column14: Tube A's catalase was used up after 2 minutes of foaming
column15: Tube A's potato was denatured by the hydrogen peroxide
column16: Tube A ran out of hydrogen peroxide
column17: Tube B was warmer
column28: The cubes are the same, so the difference is the substrate. Tube A had a quarter as much peroxide, so it ran out sooner (2 min vs 8 min). A common mistake is saying the catalase was used up; enzymes are reused, and the substrate is what runs out.
column29: What was different between the two tubes?

column9: Scientists copy DNA in a machine that heats samples to about 95 °C over and over. They use a DNA-copying enzyme from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium from hot springs, instead of a human enzyme. Why?
column14: The bacterial enzyme only works in the cold
column15: Human enzymes are too small to copy DNA, so a larger bacterial enzyme is needed
column16: The bacterial enzyme stays folded at 95 °C, but a human enzyme would denature
column17: Enzymes from hot springs are not proteins
column28: Enzymes from hot-spring bacteria are adapted to stay folded at high temperatures. A human enzyme, built for 37 °C, would unfold at 95 °C and stop working. A common mistake is thinking hot-spring enzymes aren't proteins; they are, just very heat-stable ones.
column29: Where does each enzyme normally work? What would 95 °C do to a human enzyme?

column9: A company sells pills containing amylase and claims the enzyme will be absorbed into your blood and boost the amylase in your cells. Which is the best reason to doubt this claim?
column14: Amylase is a protein, so the stomach would denature and digest it first
column15: Amylase is a sugar, so it would just be burned for energy before reaching your cells
column16: Amylase is a lipid, so it can't dissolve in water
column17: Amylase only works in plants
column28: Swallowed enzymes are proteins, so they meet strong acid and protein-digesting enzymes like pepsin. They are denatured and broken into amino acids, not absorbed whole. A common mistake is forgetting that enzymes are food molecules too.
column29: What macromolecule is amylase? What does your stomach do to that kind of molecule?

column9: Each tube has the same volume of hydrogen peroxide and the same mass of potato. Rank the tubes from MOST foam to LEAST foam after 2 minutes.
column14: Diced raw potato at room temperature
column15: One raw potato cube at room temperature
column16: One raw potato cube in an ice bath
column17: One boiled potato cube at room temperature
column28: Diced raw potato has the most exposed catalase, so it is fastest. The whole cube is next. The ice bath slows catalase but doesn't stop it. Boiled catalase is denatured, so it makes almost no foam. A common mistake is ranking the ice bath last, but cold only slows enzymes.
column29: Ask two questions for each tube: is the catalase working, and how much of it can reach the peroxide?

column9: On an energy diagram, the reactants start at 100 units of energy. Without an enzyme, the top of the hill is at 180 units. With the enzyme, the top of the hill is at 130 units. The products end at 60 units. How many units of activation energy does the reaction need WITH the enzyme?
column28: Activation energy is the climb from the reactants to the top of the hill: 130 − 100 = 30 units. A common mistake is answering 130 (the hilltop itself) or 70 (hilltop minus products).
column29: Activation energy is measured from where the reactants start to the top of the hill.

column9: A mutation changes one amino acid in the active site of a person's lactase. The new lactase no longer breaks down lactose, even at the right temperature and pH. What is the best explanation?
column14: The change altered the active site's shape, so lactose no longer fits
column15: The lactose was used up
column16: The enzyme was denatured by heat
column17: The new amino acid added extra energy to the reaction, so it went too fast
column28: A protein's amino acid order decides how it folds. Changing an amino acid in the active site can change its shape so the substrate no longer fits. A common mistake is blaming heat or pH, but the stem says those were normal.
column29: The temperature and pH were fine. What else controls an enzyme's shape?

column9: A human enzyme has activity 30 at 20 °C, 100 at 37 °C, and 20 at 50 °C. An enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium has activity 5 at 20 °C, 15 at 37 °C, 40 at 50 °C, and 100 at 75 °C. At 50 °C, which enzyme works faster, and why?
column14: The human enzyme, because it is adapted to warm bodies like ours
column15: The bacterial enzyme, because 50 °C is closer to its optimum
column16: Both work the same at 50 °C
column17: Neither works at 50 °C
column28: At 50 °C the bacterial enzyme reads 40 and the human enzyme reads 20. The human enzyme peaked at 37 °C and is losing its shape, while the bacterial enzyme is still climbing toward its 75 °C optimum. A common mistake is assuming human enzymes are best at any warm temperature.
column29: Find the 50 °C value for each enzyme, then compare each to its own peak.

column9: A tube holds 600 substrate molecules and 3 enzyme molecules. Each enzyme molecule can break down 20 substrate molecules per second. If the rate stays the same, how many seconds will it take to break down all 600 substrate molecules?
column28: Together the enzymes break down 3 × 20 = 60 molecules per second, so 600 ÷ 60 = 10 seconds. A common mistake is using only one enzyme (600 ÷ 20 = 30 s) or forgetting that the enzymes are reused.
column29: First find how many molecules ALL the enzymes break down each second.

column9: Lab results: Tube 1 (raw potato + hydrogen peroxide) = 40 mm of foam. Tube 2 (boiled potato + hydrogen peroxide) = 1 mm. Tube 3 (raw potato + water) = 0 mm. Tube 4 (hydrogen peroxide alone) = 1 mm. Select every conclusion these results support. Select all that apply.
column14: Raw potato contains something that speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide
column15: Boiling stopped the potato's catalase from working
column16: The foam comes from the hydrogen peroxide breaking down, not from the potato itself
column17: Boiling added more catalase to the potato
column18: Water is the substrate for catalase
column28: Tube 1 vs Tube 4 shows raw potato speeds the reaction; Tube 2 shows boiling stops it; Tube 3 shows potato alone makes no foam without peroxide. Boiling did not add catalase (less foam), and water is a product, not the substrate. A common mistake is ignoring the control tubes.
column29: Compare tubes two at a time. What is different between each pair?

column9: A student mixes saliva with starch at 37 °C and tests it with iodine after 10 minutes. The starch is gone. To show that the amylase in saliva (not just warmth or time) broke down the starch, what is the best control?
column14: Starch with water instead of saliva, at 37 °C for 10 minutes
column15: Starch and saliva kept at 37 °C for 20 minutes instead of 10 minutes
column16: Saliva mixed with water and no starch
column17: Starch and saliva placed in sunlight
column28: The control should match everything except the enzyme: same starch, same temperature, same time, but water instead of saliva. If that starch is still there, the amylase did the work. A common mistake is changing the time or temperature, which tests a different variable.
column29: A control keeps everything the same except the one thing being tested.

column9: Match each part of an enzyme-activity vs. temperature graph to what is happening to the enzyme.
column14: Rising left side :: Molecules move faster and collide more often
column15: Peak of the curve :: The temperature where the enzyme works fastest
column16: Steep drop just past the peak :: Active sites are starting to lose their shape
column17: Flat line near zero at the far right :: Almost every enzyme molecule is denatured
column28: On the left, warming speeds collisions. The peak is the optimum. Past it, heat begins to unfold the enzyme and the rate drops fast, until nearly all of it is denatured. A common mistake is thinking the enzyme is denatured on the left side of the graph, where it is just cold.
column29: Trace the curve from left to right and think about the enzyme's shape at each part.

column9: A glucose test strip contains the enzyme glucose oxidase. The strip changes color when glucose is present, but not when fructose or sucrose is present. Which property of enzymes makes this test useful?
column14: Enzymes are reused many times, so a little enzyme goes a long way
column15: Enzymes are made of protein
column16: Enzymes are specific: the active site fits glucose only
column17: Enzymes lower activation energy
column28: The test works because glucose oxidase reacts only with glucose; other sugars don't fit its active site, so they can't give a false result. The other choices are true about enzymes but don't explain why only glucose changes the color. A common mistake is picking a true fact that doesn't answer the question.
column29: Why does the strip ignore the other sugars?

column9: A starch molecule is a chain of 1,200 glucose units. Suppose amylase breaks the whole chain into maltose, which is 2 glucose units joined together. How many maltose molecules are made?
column28: Each maltose uses 2 glucose units, so 1,200 ÷ 2 = 600 maltose molecules. A common mistake is answering 1,200, which counts glucose units instead of maltose molecules.
column29: How many glucose units go into each maltose?

column9: A student predicts that doubling the substrate will always double the reaction rate. Her data: 1% hydrogen peroxide = 12 mm foam/min, 2% = 23, 4% = 34, 8% = 36, 16% = 36. Which evaluation is best?
column14: The prediction is fully supported, because the rate went up every time the substrate increased
column15: It roughly holds at low concentrations; once the active sites are full, the rate levels off
column16: The data show the rate goes down as substrate increases
column17: The data show the catalase was used up at 8%
column28: From 1% to 2% the rate nearly doubles, but from 8% to 16% it does not change at all. Once every active site is busy, extra substrate has to wait, so the rate levels off. A common mistake is saying the enzyme was used up; it is the active sites that are full.
column29: Compare the change from 1% to 2% with the change from 8% to 16%.

column9: Put these steps in order to show how an enzyme gets its working shape.
column14: The chain coils into helices and folds into sheets
column15: Amino acids are linked into a chain in the order set by a gene
column16: The chain folds into a full 3-D shape that includes an active site
column17: The enzyme binds its substrate
column28: Primary structure (amino acid order) → secondary (coils and sheets) → tertiary (full 3-D shape with an active site) → only then can it bind its substrate. A common mistake is putting substrate binding before the enzyme has folded; without its shape there is no active site.
column29: Start with the smallest building blocks. When does the active site exist?

column9: A student says, "A denatured enzyme can't work because it is dead." What is the best correction?
column14: The student is right; enzymes die when heated
column15: Enzymes are molecules, not living things; denaturing changes their shape
column16: Denatured enzymes still work, just more slowly, because they are only injured
column17: Enzymes can only be denatured by cold
column28: Enzymes are protein molecules, so they can't be alive or dead. Denaturing changes their 3-D shape, ruining the active site. A common mistake is using 'dead' for any enzyme that stops working.
column29: Are enzymes cells or molecules?

column9: A student mixes amylase and starch at 37 °C and tests a drop with iodine every minute. Minutes 0 to 3: blue-black. Minute 4: lighter. Minute 6: yellow-brown. What happened by minute 6?
column14: The amylase was used up
column15: The amylase broke down all or nearly all of the starch into sugars
column16: The starch turned into iodine
column17: The amylase was denatured by the 37 °C water, so the iodine color faded
column28: Iodine is blue-black when starch is present and yellow-brown when it is not. The color change shows amylase digested the starch over time. A common mistake is thinking the amylase was used up or denatured; 37 °C is ideal for human amylase, and the enzyme is reused.
column29: What does a yellow-brown iodine result mean about starch?
